topics.title: Micro vs macro: thinking in aggregates

learn.hook: One farmer in Punjab worries about the price of his wheat. The Finance Minister worries about the price of EVERYTHING at once. Welcome to macroeconomics!
points: Microeconomics studies individual units: one consumer, one firm, the market for one good like onions or cars.
Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole through aggregates: total output (GDP), total employment, the general price level, total saving and investment.

To keep things simple, macroeconomists often imagine all output as one representative good, so millions of separate markets are treated together (aggregate analysis instead of disaggregated analysis).
Economic agents are individuals or institutions that take economic decisions: households, firms, the government, and bodies like the RBI and SEBI.
Macroeconomic policy goals include higher growth, more employment, stable prices and better education and health for people.

example.q: Classify: (i) the price of tomatoes in Nashik; (ii) India's inflation rate; (iii) a firm's demand for steel; (iv) total employment in India.
steps: Ask: is it about one unit/market or the whole economy?
(i) one good's market → micro; (iii) one firm → micro
(ii) the general price level → macro; (iv) employment in the whole economy → macro
example.answer: (i) and (iii) are micro; (ii) and (iv) are macro

learn.reallife: When the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee meets, it looks at aggregate inflation and GDP growth for all of India, not the price of one brand of biscuits.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a macroeconomic variable?
options: The price of a kilo of potatoes
The output of one sugar mill
The demand for one brand of shoes
quiz.explain: Macroeconomics deals with aggregates for the whole economy; the general price level is an aggregate.
steps: Asked: which variable is an aggregate for the whole economy?
Macro studies aggregates; one good, one mill or one brand is a single unit (micro)
The general price level covers all goods in the economy
Answer: The general price level
quiz.mistake: Treats any price as macro, even the price of a single good

quiz.q: Macroeconomic analysis often treats all goods as a single 'representative good' mainly because
options: it simplifies the study of the whole economy by aggregating many markets
every good in reality has the same price
the government produces only one good
micro-level data are not collected in India
quiz.explain: Aggregation lets economists talk about total output and the general price level without studying each market separately.
steps: Asked: why treat all output as one representative good?
Key idea: aggregation lets us study the whole economy without each market separately
It is a simplifying assumption, not a claim that all goods have the same price
Answer: it simplifies the study of the whole economy by aggregating many markets
quiz.mistake: Takes a simplifying assumption to be a literal fact

quiz.q: Which of these is an economic agent?
options: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
quiz.explain: Economic agents are individuals or institutions that take economic decisions. SEBI takes decisions regulating the share market.
steps: Economic agent = an individual or institution that takes economic decisions
Rice, a plough and the monsoon do not take decisions
SEBI takes decisions to regulate the share market
Answer: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
quiz.mistake: Confuses goods or natural events with decision-makers

quiz.q: Which pair correctly shows a micro and a macro question?
options: Micro: price of cotton; Macro: rate of inflation
Micro: national income; Macro: price of tea
Micro: aggregate demand; Macro: a firm's output
Micro: total employment; Macro: a worker's wage
quiz.explain: Price of one good is micro; the overall inflation rate is macro.
steps: Micro = one unit or one market; macro = the whole economy
Price of cotton is one market (micro); the inflation rate is the general price level (macro)
The other options put an aggregate under micro or a single unit under macro
Answer: Micro: price of cotton; Macro: rate of inflation
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which level each variable belongs to

quiz.q: Which is NOT usually listed as a macroeconomic policy goal?
options: Maximising the profit of one particular firm
quiz.explain: Macro policy aims at goals for the economy as a whole; one firm's profit is a micro concern.
steps: Macro policy goals: growth, employment, stable prices, education and health
These are goals for the economy as a whole
One particular firm's profit is a micro concern
Answer: Maximising the profit of one particular firm
quiz.mistake: Thinks government macro policy targets individual firms

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Macroeconomics studies the determination of national income and employment. Reason (R): Macroeconomics deals with aggregates of the whole economy.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: National income and employment are aggregates, which is exactly why macroeconomics studies them.
steps: A: macro studies national income and employment — true
R: macro deals with aggregates of the whole economy — true
National income and employment are aggregates, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Fails to link the scope of macro to its use of aggregates

quiz.q: A study of how a rise in the price of petrol affects the demand for scooters is an example of
quiz.explain: It examines individual markets (petrol and scooters), so it is a micro study.
steps: Asked: is this about one market or the whole economy?
It looks at the market for petrol and the demand for scooters — individual markets
Answer: microeconomics
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything involving petrol, a big commodity, must be macro

quiz.q: Why do macroeconomists study aggregate rather than disaggregated data?
options: Because individual data are always wrong
Because aggregates are always larger, so more important
Because macroeconomics ignores households and firms
To understand how the economy as a whole behaves, such as total output and the price level
quiz.explain: Aggregates show the overall picture (growth, inflation, jobs) that policy-makers need.
steps: Aggregates show total output, total employment and the general price level
Policy-makers need this overall picture; macro adds up individual agents, it does not ignore them
Answer: To understand how the economy as a whole behaves, such as total output and the price level
quiz.mistake: Thinks macro ignores individual agents rather than adding them up

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'My uncle studies the price of seeds. My aunt studies India's GDP. Aren't they both just doing economics?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Uncle studies one market (micro) and aunt studies aggregates for the whole economy (macro). Both are economics, at different levels!
teach.nudge: You've told me what uncle does. What makes aunt's work different? Think about the whole economy.

revise.summary: Microeconomics studies individual units such as one consumer, firm or market, while macroeconomics studies the whole economy through aggregates like GDP, employment and the general price level.
focus: Classify a variable or question as micro or macro
Name economic agents and macro policy goals
remember: Macro aggregates: total output (GDP), total employment, general price level, total saving and investment
Economic agents: households, firms, government, bodies like RBI and SEBI
Macro goals: growth, employment, stable prices, education and health
traps: The price of one good is micro, not macro
Macro adds up individual agents; it does not ignore them
A 'representative good' is a simplification, not a fact

topics.title: Classical economics and the Great Depression

learn.hook: In 1929 the world's richest economy hit a wall: by 1933 one in every four American workers who wanted a job could not find one.
points: Adam Smith, author of 'The Wealth of Nations' (1776), is regarded as the founder of modern economics. Classical economists who followed him believed in free markets.
Classical view: if markets are left free, wages and prices adjust so that all who want work at the going wage find it; the economy tends to full employment by itself.
The Great Depression began in 1929. In the USA, output of goods and services fell sharply and the unemployment rate rose from about 3% to about 25% by 1933.
Unemployment rate = (number of people looking for work but jobless ÷ labour force) × 100, where the labour force = people working + people seeking work.
The long, deep slump showed that markets did not quickly correct themselves, which challenged the classical belief.

example.q: In a town, 1,840 people have jobs and 160 people are actively looking for work but jobless. Find the unemployment rate.
steps: Labour force = employed + unemployed = 1,840 + 160 = 2,000
Unemployment rate = 160 ÷ 2,000 × 100

learn.reallife: During the COVID-19 lockdown in 2020, India's unemployment rate jumped sharply, reminding economists why the Great Depression made macroeconomics necessary.

games.title: Story of the Depression
games.prompt: Put the events in time order
items: Adam Smith's 'The Wealth of Nations' is published

items.q: Labour force 400, rate 25%. How many unemployed?

quiz.q: Who wrote 'The Wealth of Nations' (1776) and is regarded as the founder of modern economics?
quiz.explain: Adam Smith published 'The Wealth of Nations' in 1776; the classical tradition grew from his ideas.
steps: 'The Wealth of Nations' was published in 1776
Its author, Adam Smith, is regarded as the founder of modern economics
Keynes (1936) is linked with the birth of macroeconomics, not of economics
Answer: Adam Smith
quiz.mistake: Confuses the founder of economics with the founder of macroeconomics (Keynes)

quiz.q: According to the classical economists, an economy left to free markets would
options: tend to full employment automatically as wages and prices adjust
need the government to fix all prices
never produce more than it consumes
quiz.explain: Classical economists believed flexible wages and prices would clear the labour and goods markets.
steps: Classical economists believed in free markets
With free markets, wages and prices adjust so all who want work at the going wage find it
So the economy moves to full employment by itself
Answer: tend to full employment automatically as wages and prices adjust
quiz.mistake: Assigns Keynes's view to the classical economists

quiz.q: During the Great Depression the unemployment rate in the USA rose from about 3% to about
quiz.explain: From 1929 to 1933 the US unemployment rate rose from about 3% to about 25%.
steps: Great Depression: began in 1929
US unemployment rose from about 3% to about 25% by 1933
Answer: 25%
quiz.mistake: Remembers that unemployment rose but not how severe it became

quiz.q: In an economy 9,500 people are employed and 500 are seeking work but unemployed. What is the unemployment rate?
quiz.explain: Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100 = 500 ÷ 10,000 × 100 = 5%.
steps: Answer: 5%
quiz.mistake: Divides by the employed (500/9,500) instead of the whole labour force

quiz.q: Which people are counted in the labour force?
options: Those who are working and those who are looking for work
Only those who are looking for work
quiz.explain: The labour force includes the employed plus the unemployed who are actively seeking work.
steps: Labour force = people working + people seeking work
Children, retired people and others not seeking work are excluded
Answer: Those who are working and those who are looking for work
quiz.mistake: Leaves out job-seekers or includes children and retired people

quiz.q: The labour force of a district is 80,000 and its unemployment rate is 6%. How many people are unemployed?
steps: Answer: 4800
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of finding a percentage, or slips a zero

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The Great Depression weakened faith in the classical theory. Reason (R): Output and employment stayed low for years instead of recovering quickly on their own.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Classical theory predicted quick self-correction; the long slump contradicted that, so R explains A.
steps: A: the Depression weakened faith in classical theory — true
R: output and employment stayed low for years — true
Classical theory predicted quick self-correction; the long slump contradicted it, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the failure of self-correction with the loss of faith

quiz.q: When did the Great Depression begin?
quiz.explain: The Great Depression started in 1929; 1936 is the year Keynes's General Theory appeared.
steps: The Great Depression began in 1929 (the USA)
1936 is the year of Keynes's General Theory, not the start of the Depression
Answer: 1929
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the start of the Depression with Keynes's book

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If markets fix themselves, why did so many people stay jobless after 1929?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The classical economists expected self-correction, but the Great Depression kept unemployment near 25% for years. Theory met reality!
teach.nudge: You mentioned the jobless people. What did the classical economists believe would happen on its own?

revise.summary: Classical economists following Adam Smith believed free markets reach full employment by themselves. The Great Depression from 1929, when US unemployment rose from about 3% to about 25%, challenged this belief.
focus: Know Adam Smith and the classical view
Know the Great Depression's dates and unemployment figures
remember: Great Depression began 1929; US unemployment about 3% → about 25% by 1933
Labour force = employed + those seeking work
traps: Divide by the labour force, not by the employed
The labour force excludes people not seeking work

learn.hook: One book in 1936 split economics into two branches. Its author, John Maynard Keynes, also helped design the post-war world money system at Bretton Woods.
points: John Maynard Keynes, a British economist, published 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money' in 1936.
Keynes argued that output and employment depend on aggregate (effective) demand, and that an economy can stay stuck with unemployment for a long time.
His approach studied the economy as a whole, so 1936 is taken as the birth of macroeconomics as a separate branch.
A capitalist economy has: (a) private ownership of the means of production, (b) production mainly for sale in the market, and (c) sale and purchase of labour services at a wage rate.
In a capitalist economy, firms run by capitalists hire wage workers and produce goods for profit.

example.q: A village has a potter who makes pots only for his own family and a factory owner in Morbi who hires 200 workers on wages to make tiles for sale. Which shows capitalist production?
steps: Check the three features: private ownership, production for market sale, wage labour
The potter: no market sale, no hired labour
The Morbi factory: private owner, tiles sold, workers paid wages

learn.reallife: Modern India is a mixed economy, but large parts of it, such as private IT firms in Bengaluru hiring engineers for a salary to sell services worldwide, work on capitalist lines.

games.title: Keynes or not?
items: It appeared in 1936, during the Depression years.
Keynes argued that output depends on aggregate demand.
Effective demand is at the heart of his theory.
Keynes believed the economy always returns quickly to full employment.
That was the classical view; Keynes said unemployment can persist.
Production for one's own use is a feature of a capitalist economy.
Capitalist production is for sale in the market.
In a capitalist economy, labour services are bought and sold at a wage rate.
Wage labour is one of the three features.
In a capitalist economy, the means of production are mostly owned by the state.

items.text: In a capitalist economy the means of production are ___ owned.

quiz.q: 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money' was written by
quiz.explain: Keynes published the General Theory in 1936.
steps: 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money' (1936)
Written by the British economist John Maynard Keynes
Answer: John Maynard Keynes
quiz.mistake: Credits the founder of classical economics instead

quiz.q: In which year was Keynes's General Theory published?
quiz.explain: It was published in 1936, seven years after the Depression began.
steps: Keynes's General Theory came out after the Depression began (1929)
It was published in 1936
Answer: 1936
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the start of the Depression (1929) or Bretton Woods (1944)

quiz.q: Keynes's main idea was that the level of output and employment is determined by
options: the money wage set by trade unions alone
the size of a country's land
the amount of gold held by banks
quiz.explain: Keynes said aggregate demand decides how much is produced and how many people are employed.
steps: Keynes: output and employment depend on aggregate (effective) demand
So low demand can keep the economy stuck with unemployment
Answer: aggregate (effective) demand
quiz.mistake: Thinks supply-side factors alone fix output in the short run

quiz.q: Which is NOT a feature of a capitalist economy?
options: Private ownership of means of production
Production for sale in the market
quiz.explain: Capitalist production is for the market, not for one's own use.
steps: Capitalist features: private ownership, production for sale in the market, wage labour
Production for self-consumption is not production for the market
Answer: Production mainly for self-consumption
quiz.mistake: Mixes up a subsistence economy with a capitalist one

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Macroeconomics emerged as a separate branch after Keynes. Reason (R): Keynes analysed the working of the economy as a whole, focusing on aggregate demand.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Keynes's whole-economy approach is exactly why his work founded macroeconomics.
steps: A: macro became a separate branch after Keynes (1936) — true
R: Keynes studied the economy as a whole, focusing on aggregate demand — true
That whole-economy approach is why his work founded macro, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Sees both as true but misses the cause-effect link

quiz.q: A capitalist in NCERT's sense is a person who
options: owns a firm, hires workers and sells output for profit
works for wages in a factory
grows food only for his family
quiz.explain: Capitalists own the means of production and hire wage labour to produce for the market.
steps: Capitalist: owns the means of production (a firm)
Hires wage workers and sells output in the market for profit
A wage worker is the one hired, not the capitalist
Answer: owns a firm, hires workers and sells output for profit
quiz.mistake: Confuses the capitalist with the wage worker

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the Keynesian view compared with the classical view?
options: Unemployment can persist for a long time unless demand increases
Prices are the only thing that matters
quiz.explain: Keynes rejected automatic quick self-correction and stressed demand.
steps: Classical view: markets clear and correct themselves quickly
Keynes: an economy can stay stuck with unemployment for long unless aggregate demand rises
Answer: Unemployment can persist for a long time unless demand increases
quiz.mistake: Assigns the classical view to Keynes

quiz.q: In a capitalist economy, the price paid for labour services is called the
quiz.explain: Labour is bought and sold at the wage rate; rent, interest and profit go to other factors.
steps: In a capitalist economy labour services are bought and sold
The price paid for labour services is the wage rate (rent → land, interest → capital, profit → entrepreneur)
Answer: wage rate
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the rewards of different factors

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Who is this Keynes everyone talks about, and what is a capitalist economy anyway?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Keynes's 1936 General Theory said demand drives output, and capitalism means private owners hiring wage labour to produce for the market. Got it!
teach.nudge: Nice start on Keynes. Can you also tell me the features of a capitalist economy?

revise.summary: Keynes's General Theory (1936) said output and employment depend on aggregate demand and that unemployment can persist, giving birth to macroeconomics. A capitalist economy has private ownership, production for the market and wage labour.
focus: Know Keynes's book, year and main idea
List the features of a capitalist economy
remember: Keynes, 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money', 1936
Output and employment depend on aggregate (effective) demand
Capitalist economy: private ownership, production for sale, wage labour
traps: Don't give Keynes the classical belief in quick self-correction
Production for self-use is not capitalist production
The price of labour is the wage rate, not profit or rent

topics.title: Factors of production and the entrepreneur

learn.hook: Every rupee of income in India ends up in one of four pockets: rent, wages, interest or profit. Which pocket is yours?
points: Four factors of production: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship.
Their rewards (factor payments): land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest, entrepreneurship earns profit.
The entrepreneur organises the other factors, takes decisions and bears the risk of loss; profit is the reward for this risk-taking.
Investment expenditure is spending by firms on new machines, buildings and stocks; it adds to the productive capacity of the economy.

example.q: Raghav runs a dhaba on a highway. He rents the plot for ₹20,000 a month, pays cooks ₹45,000, pays ₹5,000 interest on a bank loan, and keeps what is left. Name each factor payment.
steps: Plot (land) → ₹20,000 is rent
Cooks (labour) → ₹45,000 is wages
Bank loan (capital) → ₹5,000 is interest
Raghav (entrepreneur, bears the risk) → the remainder is profit
example.answer: Rent, wages, interest and profit respectively

learn.reallife: Startup founders in Bengaluru are entrepreneurs: they combine venture capital, rented office space and hired coders, and they earn profit only if the risk pays off.

games.title: Which factor payment is it?
items: Surplus kept by a startup owner

quiz.q: The reward for entrepreneurship is
quiz.explain: The entrepreneur bears risk and earns the residual surplus called profit.
steps: Factor rewards: land → rent, labour → wages, capital → interest
Entrepreneurship → profit, the reward for bearing risk
Answer: profit
quiz.mistake: Mixes up factor rewards

quiz.q: Interest is the reward paid for the use of
quiz.explain: Capital earns interest; land earns rent.
steps: Factor rewards: land → rent, labour → wages, entrepreneurship → profit
Capital → interest
Answer: capital
quiz.mistake: Mixes up rent and interest

quiz.q: Which role is unique to the entrepreneur?
options: Providing physical labour on the shop floor
Bearing the risk of loss while organising production
quiz.explain: Risk-bearing and decision-making mark the entrepreneur; profit rewards it.
steps: The entrepreneur organises land, labour and capital and takes decisions
Only the entrepreneur bears the risk of loss; profit rewards this
Labour, lending or owning land alone are other factors' roles
Answer: Bearing the risk of loss while organising production
quiz.mistake: Thinks any worker or lender is an entrepreneur

quiz.q: Investment expenditure by firms on new machines
options: has no effect on future output
is the same as consumption expenditure
adds to the productive capacity of the economy
quiz.explain: New capital goods raise the economy's ability to produce in future.
steps: Investment = spending by firms on new machines, buildings and stocks
New capital goods let the economy produce more in future
Answer: adds to the productive capacity of the economy
quiz.mistake: Confuses investment with consumption

quiz.q: A firm pays ₹3 lakh as wages, ₹1 lakh as rent and ₹50,000 as interest. Its revenue is ₹6 lakh and it has no other costs. What is the profit (in ₹)?
steps: Total factor payments other than profit = 3,00,000 + 1,00,000 + 50,000 = 4,50,000
Answer: 150000
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract one of the factor payments

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The entrepreneur earns profit. Reason (R): Profit is the reward for bearing risk and uncertainty in production.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Profit exists because the entrepreneur bears risk, so R explains A.
steps: A: the entrepreneur earns profit — true
R: profit is the reward for bearing risk and uncertainty — true
Profit exists because the entrepreneur bears risk, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see risk-bearing as the source of profit

quiz.q: Rent is the reward for
quiz.explain: Land (natural resources) earns rent.
steps: Factor rewards: capital → interest, labour → wages, organisation → profit
Land (natural resources) → rent
Answer: land
quiz.mistake: Thinks rent is paid for any hired thing, including money capital

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of investment expenditure?
options: A textile mill buying new looms
quiz.explain: Buying capital goods like looms is investment; the others are consumption or transfers.
steps: Investment = buying capital goods that add to productive capacity
Vegetables and school fees are consumption; pensions are transfers
New looms are capital goods for the mill
Answer: A textile mill buying new looms
quiz.mistake: Thinks any spending is investment

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Who gets rent, who gets wages, and why does the boss get profit?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Land gets rent, labour wages, capital interest, and the risk-taking entrepreneur gets profit. Four factors, four rewards!
teach.nudge: You listed some rewards. Why does the entrepreneur deserve profit? Think about risk.

revise.summary: The four factors of production are land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship, rewarded by rent, wages, interest and profit. Profit is the entrepreneur's reward for bearing risk.
focus: Match each factor with its reward
Find profit as the remainder after other factor payments
remember: Land → rent; labour → wages; capital → interest; entrepreneurship → profit
Entrepreneur organises production and bears risk
Investment: spending on new machines, buildings and stocks
traps: Don't mix up rent (land) and interest (capital)
Buying vegetables or paying fees is consumption, not investment
Subtract every factor payment before calling the rest profit

learn.hook: Your chai purchase, a GST payment and an Infosys export bill to the USA all belong to different 'sectors' of the same economy.
points: Macroeconomics groups economic agents into four sectors: households, firms, government and the external sector (rest of the world).
Households supply factor services (labour, land, capital) and buy consumer goods; firms hire factors and produce goods and services.
Government makes laws, enforces contracts, taxes people and firms, spends on public services and infrastructure, and regulates economic activity.
External sector: exports (goods sold abroad), imports (goods bought from abroad) and capital flows (foreign investment and borrowing).
A closed economy has no external sector; an open economy trades and has capital flows with other countries.

example.q: Assign each transaction to its sector: (i) Tata Motors hires workers; (ii) a family buys a fridge; (iii) the Centre collects income tax; (iv) India imports crude oil.
steps: (i) a producing unit hiring factors → firms
(ii) buying consumer goods → households
(iii) taxation → government
(iv) trade with other countries → external sector

learn.reallife: Remittances from Indians working in the Gulf and software exports to the USA connect India's households and firms with the external sector every day.

games.title: Which sector?
items: Foreign investment in an Indian startup

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the four sectors in the simple macro model?
quiz.explain: The four sectors are households, firms, government and the external sector.
steps: Four sectors: households, firms, government, external sector
Trade unions are not one of these four sectors
Answer: Trade unions
quiz.mistake: Thinks any organised group is a sector

quiz.q: Which sector supplies factor services such as labour?
quiz.explain: Households own factors of production and supply their services to firms.
steps: Households own factors of production (labour, land, capital)
They supply factor services to firms
Answer: Households
quiz.mistake: Thinks firms supply labour

quiz.q: Imports, exports and capital flows belong to the
quiz.explain: The external sector covers dealings with the rest of the world.
steps: Dealings with the rest of the world: exports, imports, capital flows
These form the external sector
Answer: external sector
quiz.mistake: Places trade under government because of customs duty

quiz.q: Which of these is a function of the government sector?
options: Selling goods for private profit only
Imposing taxes and spending on public services
quiz.explain: Government makes laws, taxes and spends, and regulates the economy.
steps: Government: makes laws, enforces contracts, taxes, spends on public services, regulates
Profit-seeking sale is firms; supplying labour is households
Answer: Imposing taxes and spending on public services
quiz.mistake: Confuses government with firms

quiz.q: An economy that has no dealings with the rest of the world is called a
quiz.explain: A closed economy has no external sector.
steps: Closed economy: no external sector (no trade or capital flows)
Open economy: trades with other countries
Answer: closed economy
quiz.mistake: Mixes up open/closed with mixed/dual

quiz.q: A foreign company buying shares of an Indian firm is an example of
options: a capital flow in the external sector
quiz.explain: Purchase of Indian assets by foreigners is a capital inflow.
steps: Foreign purchase of Indian shares is not trade in goods
It is foreign investment, i.e. a capital flow in the external sector
Answer: a capital flow in the external sector
quiz.mistake: Treats every foreign dealing as trade in goods

quiz.q: Assertion (A): In the four-sector model, firms make payments to households. Reason (R): Households supply factor services to firms.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Firms pay wages, rent, interest and profit because households provide the factors.
steps: A: firms make payments to households — true
R: households supply factor services to firms — true
Firms pay wages, rent, interest and profit because they use households' factors, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Misses why factor payments flow from firms to households

quiz.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Households: producing for sale with hired workers

steps: Households supply factors; firms produce; government taxes and enforces laws; external sector trades
Only 'Government: enforcing laws and contracts' is a correct pair
Answer: Government: enforcing laws and contracts
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the roles of the sectors

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Who are the four big players in an economy, and what does each one do?'
teach.praise: Tweet-tweet! Households, firms, government and the external sector: that's the full macro team!
teach.nudge: You named some players. Did you leave out anyone, like the rest of the world?

revise.summary: The macro model has four sectors: households, firms, government and the external sector. Households supply factors, firms produce, government taxes, spends and regulates, and the external sector covers trade and capital flows.
focus: Assign transactions to the right sector
Know the role of each sector
remember: Four sectors: households, firms, government, external sector
External sector: exports, imports, capital flows
Closed economy: no external sector; open economy: trades with the world
traps: Trade unions are not one of the four sectors
Foreign buying of Indian shares is a capital flow, not trade in goods
Firms pay factor incomes to households, not the other way round
